newsitem.title: UK: Euro-bourses relaxed ahead of U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Euro-bourses relaxed ahead of U.S. election.

text.p: Equity, currency and bond markets across Europe were tranquil by midday as investors expected President Bill Clinton to be re-elected after Tuesday's U.S. ballot, dealers and strategists said.
"The election is not having any impact on the German (share) market," said Byron Gilliam, trader at stockbroker Ballmaier & Schultz in Frankfurt.
"People here are pretty apathetic. It might be an excuse not to do much but everyone expects Clinton to get in again."

Gilliam said German investors would focus on upcoming third-quarter corporate earnings as well as the direction of the German bund rather than the U.S. general election, where President Clinton holds a commanding lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole.
British investors were also more interested in domestic matters rather than Tuesday's vote, according to Steve Wright, equities strategist at London-based brokers BZW.
"The result is a foregone conclusion," Wright said. "Our market is concerned about interest rates and the strength of sterling."

The pound has appreciated by around eight percent over the last three months raising concerns that UK corporates with large foreign holdings, could see revenues dip when translated from dollars, yen or marks back into sterling, Wright said.
Dealers in Paris were more cautious ahead of Tuesday's U.S. vote where seats in the entire lower House of Representatives and one-third of the upper house, the Senate, are also up for grabs.

"The market is still bullish but the American election holds some uncertainties," said one trader in Paris. "If you take as a given Clinton's re-election, we are still asking ourselves about the composition of the House and the Senate and the chances of a change in the balance of power."

U.S. political analysts say many congressional races are so close that President Clinton's Democratic Party could win back control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Republicans won both in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.

With the exception of President Clinton's first two-years in office, no President has been able to count on support of Congress to push through legislation of one party, since President Lyndon Johnson in the 1960's.

Fear that a Democrat clean sweep of both Congress and the White House could translate into more government spending or protectionist trade policies kept many currency players on the sidelines on Monday.

"I think those fears are overdone," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International in London. Stamenkovic believes that even if the Democrats did win both electoral prizes, they would be unlikely to alter fiscal policy dramatically.
U.S. treasuries were muted in London, as the market braced itself for the start of quarterly refunding and the U.S. elections, strategists said.

They said that although a victory for President Clinton has been discounted, bond investors are concerned that a Democrat-controlled Congress would exercise less fiscal restraint than the Republicans.
"If the Democrats do win control of the House, we'll see a rise in the long bond yield of 25 basis points," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi in London.
